title: Is Salesforce Still The Business You Bought?
detail:
Is Salesforce Still The Business You Bought?
Trefis Team

CRM
MSFT
ORCL
ADBE
NOW
Explore stocks on Coinbase
Trading disclosure
Image from Pixabay

If you hold Salesforce (CRM), you likely bought into a subscription software provider known for steady growth and reliable cash generation. During its fiscal Q2 2027 earnings call in August, management noted that a $25 billion accelerated share repurchase was still under way. Has a buyback of that size changed the company behind your shares?

Partly: Salesforce's Balance Sheet Has Changed

While the core software operation looks much as it did a year ago, the underlying balance sheet looks starkly different. Debt accounted for 38.1% of the company's assets during fiscal Q2 2027, the latest reported quarter. For the fourteen years prior to the past year, that metric typically sat around 14.8%. In absolute terms, Salesforce held total debt of $41.7 billion at the end of the quarter. That compares with just $11.4 billion in cash and short-term investments.

Why Is Salesforce's Debt So High?

Salesforce is currently spending more on its own stock than its operations generate. The company deployed $35.1 billion for buybacks over the last twelve months, yet its free cash flow over the same period came in at $15.2 billion. Bridging that shortfall required Salesforce to rely on existing cash reserves or tap debt markets. During the August call, management said it expects to buy back at least 14% of the shares outstanding through the accelerated program.

The underlying business still resembles the enterprise of a year ago. Salesforce recorded an operating margin of 22% over the last twelve months, climbing slightly from 21% a year earlier. Management noted that customer attrition sits near its lowest level ever. Meanwhile, fiscal Q2 2027 revenue grew 11% from a year earlier in constant currency.

What Do You Get For Salesforce's Debt?

Shareholders walk away with a larger slice of the business. Salesforce reported 821 million diluted shares in the latest reported quarter, a drop from 962 million a year earlier. Each remaining share now holds a claim on a larger portion of the profit. The company has also acquired this stock at a discount to current trading levels. Management noted in August that shares purchased so far under the accelerated program cost an average of $176 each, below the $229.13 price where the stock now trades.

The tradeoff comes in the form of the debt Salesforce now carries. After subtracting cash, Salesforce carries debt equal to about 1.8 times a year of its earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortization. The company must service interest on those obligations before any cash can reach shareholders.

Credit: Getty Images

Stocks closed mixed in Monday's quiet session. While the equity market was open, the bond market was closed for the Columbus Day and Indigenous Peoples' Day holidays. No earnings and economic reports were scheduled for release today, though the action picks up starting tomorrow.

At the close, the blue-chip Dow Jones Industrial Average was up 0.4% at 51,850, as Salesforce (CRM) climbed 2.1% on a double upgrade from BofA Securities analyst Tal Liani.

Liani lifted his rating on the Dow Jones stock to Buy from Underperform, the equivalent of Sell, and raised his price target to $285 from $160. Salesforce, which is down 12% year to date, hasn't traded near $285 since May 2025.

"Our prior concern centered on AI-driven disintermediation," writes Liani in a note to clients. "However, conversations with CIOs and other market participants suggest that large enterprises (more than small-to-medium-sized businesses) are unlikely to replace platforms that house their business logic, data, workflows and compliance frameworks."

Looking for more timely stock market news to help gauge the health of your portfolio? Sign up for Closing Bell, our free newsletter that's delivered straight to your inbox at the close of each trading day.

And AI, Liani adds, "should deepen dependence on these platforms." He believes that Salesforce has a credible AI strategy and is poised for strong free cash flow generation.

Track all markets on TradingView

The bull market celebrates its fourth anniversary

The broader S&P 500 (-0.06% at 7,807) and tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite (-0.4% at 27,245), meanwhile, finished slightly lower Monday.

The Dow is roughly 4.5% below its record high from early August, while the S&P 500 and Nasdaq are perched not far from the all-time peaks they notched last week.

Today marked the fourth anniversary of the current bull market. The S&P 500 has gained roughly 118% on a price return basis, "surpassing the historical average of ~90% and ranking as the third-strongest bull market since 1945. Along the way, it has produced 124 record highs, more than double the average (~50) of the seven prior bull markets that lasted at least four years," says Raymond James Chief Investment Officer Larry Adam.

Adam adds that volatility has remained below average over the past four years, while earnings growth, rather than multiple expansion, has fueled the bull market's returns.

And history suggests there's more room to run. According to Adam, the average bull market lasts about five and a half years, with the fifth year averaging roughly 15% annually and finishing positive 90% of the time.

The Dow Jones Industrial Average (DJINDICES:^DJI) rose 0.38% to 51,851 as investors favored value-oriented sectors, while the S&P 500 (SNPINDEX:^GSPC) slipped 0.06% to 7,807 and the Nasdaq Composite (NASDAQINDEX:^IXIC) fell 0.44% to 27,246 on technology sector weakness.

Gold prices fell 0.64% to $4,167.56 as of U.S. market close, and the 10-Year Treasury yield edged up 0.01% to 5.24%. Communication services and consumer defensive stocks led all sectors, while technology stocks lagged.

Today's biggest moves

Salesforce gained on an analyst upgrade, and Figs surged over 12% as the healthcare apparel attracted further investor attention -- the stock is now up over 30% in the past five days. Sandisk tumbled more than 6% on memory competition concerns, and Lumentum Holdings fell almost 10%, erasing last week's gains as investors retreated from artificial intelligence (AI) industry stocks. On the flip side, Meta Platforms shares increased following the launch of Muse Wonder, its latest AI model.

What this means for investors

It's the fourth anniversary of the S&P 500, which has gained over 120% since Oct. 12, 2022, and investors will be watching the final reporting season of the year for resilience and signs that the rally still has further to run. Financial stocks gained ahead of key earnings from major banks this week. It will be a high-impact week, with key inflation data due and oil prices rising. Bond markets were closed today.

Against that backdrop, Tech stocks came under pressure, weighing on the Nasdaq while the Dow gained as investors rotated into cautious sectors. Semiconductor names like like Marvell Technology (NASDAQ:MRVL) and Semtech (NASDAQ:SMTC) declined on renewed valuation jitters.

title: Has Salesforce (CRM) Fallen Far Enough To Look Undervalued On Earnings?
detail:
Has Salesforce (CRM) Fallen Far Enough To Look Undervalued On Earnings?
Bailey Pemberton
Mon, October 12, 2026 at 10:08 AM PDT 4 min read
CRM
Trade CRM on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

Salesforce has leaned hard into artificial intelligence and large customer wins, yet the share price is still down from where it was five years ago, which puts fresh focus on whether current earnings really back up today's valuation. With the stock recently closing at US$229.13 and a mixed return profile, the central issue for you is how much of the AI and platform story is already reflected in the multiple the market is placing on its profits.

Over the past 5 years, Salesforce shares have declined about 20.0%. This raises the question of whether that weaker long run outcome now lines up more closely with what its earnings can justify.

Recent moves to acquire Listen Labs and Loops, deepen AI partnerships, and secure long term contracts such as the HMRC CRM deal can influence expectations for earnings growth, cash generation and the timing of those cash flows that underpins any valuation built on profits.

There is a second opinion on Salesforce worth weighing. See what analysts think Salesforce's shares could be worth.

The issue now is whether Salesforce's current price can be explained by the earnings it is generating today and what investors expect those profits to look like over time.

If you want more ideas with a similar AI edge while you weigh Salesforce on its earnings, a focused screen of 38 AI small caps can be a useful next step in your research.

Does Salesforce Look Undervalued on Earnings?

For Salesforce, the P/E ratio is a straightforward way to see what you are paying for each dollar of current earnings. The stock trades on roughly 19.5x earnings, using the latest figure, which is well below the broader software industry average of about 31.0x and also under the peer group average near 48.0x. Because the recent Listen Labs and Loops deals reinforce the AI angle, that gap indicates the market is not assigning Salesforce the same earnings multiple as many software rivals that are also emphasizing automation.

The tailored fair multiple for Salesforce, which adjusts for its growth profile, margins, sector and size, is above the current 19.5x. On this framework, the stock appears to trade at a discount, even after AI-centric news, large CRM contracts and the share buyback have kept attention on the company. For you as an investor, the key question is whether the business quality and earnings path justify that lower P/E relative to what the model suggests as a more typical earnings multiple.
